paragraphs.heading: A long rise, now faster
paragraphs.text: Sea level has been climbing, broadly, since the Last Glacial Maximum ended about 20,000 years ago. From 1901 to 2018 the world's average sea level went up 15–25 cm, gaining 2.3 mm a year since the 1970s. That pace beat anything seen in at least the past 3,000 years. In 2013–2022 it sped up again, to 4.62 mm a year.

paragraphs.heading: Why the water is rising
paragraphs.text: Human-caused climate change is the main reason the rise keeps accelerating. Between 1993 and 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers supplied 44% of the rise, and another 42% came from thermal expansion of the water. The sea also responds slowly, trailing temperature changes by decades. So the rise will keep speeding up until 2050 because of warming that has already happened, and after that the path depends on how much greenhouse gas people release.

paragraphs.heading: Two possible futures
paragraphs.text: If emissions are cut very deeply, the rise would slow between 2050 and 2100. Seas could then gain 30 cm to 1.0 m between the early 2020s and 2100. With high emissions the rise would speed up further, reaching 50 cm or even 1.9 m by 2100. Over the next 2000 years, holding warming to today's 1.5 °C would still mean 2–3 m, while a peak of 5 °C would mean 19–22 metres.

paragraphs.heading: Who feels it
paragraphs.text: Every coastal population on Earth is affected, through flooding, bigger storm surges, king tides and greater exposure to tsunamis. Knock-on effects include the loss of coastal ecosystems such as mangrove swamps, possibly lower crop yields as irrigation water grows saltier, and damaged ports that disrupt trade by sea. By 2050, places home to tens of millions of people will face flooding every year. Without sharp cuts in emissions, that could grow to hundreds of millions later in the century.

paragraphs.heading: Uneven from place to place
paragraphs.text: How bad the harm gets depends heavily on local conditions such as tidal range and subsidence, which is land sinking or settling. Elsewhere land is rising instead, through post-glacial rebound as the weight of melted ice comes off. In the United States, the rise by the end of the century is likely to be two to three times the global average. Still, twelve of the twenty most exposed countries are in Asia, among them Indonesia, Bangladesh and the Philippines. In the near term the hardest hit will be low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands, including atolls, many of which will become uninhabitable later this century.

paragraphs.heading: Ways to adapt
paragraphs.text: Societies have several ways to adapt. Hard approaches include managed retreat, accommodating coastal change, and building defences such as seawalls. Soft approaches include rehabilitating dunes and nourishing beaches. Sometimes these go together and sometimes one must be chosen over another, and poorer nations may find it harder to adopt the same measures as richer ones. Research suggests that communities with fewer social and economic resources often face more flood risk and have less means to adapt or move.
